source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: On GPQA Diamond, a think-step-by-step prompt gives small or no gains for reasoning-trained models and costs 20-80% more time. For non-reasoning models it mostly lifts the average but breaks some questions the model got right. Many models already write a short chain unprompted, so the prompt adds little.
numbers: 198 questions x 25 trials = 4,950 runs per prompt per model, temperature 0. Reasoning models, step-by-step vs direct, average rating: o3-mini +2.9 points (p=.024), o4-mini +3.1 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -3.3 (p=.005); Flash 2.5 on the 100%-correct metric -13.1 points. Non-reasoning, step-by-step vs forced-direct: Gemini Flash 2.0 +13.5, Sonnet 3.5 +11.7, GPT-4o-mini +4.4 (p=.067, ns). Step-by-step vs unprompted default: Flash 2.0 +6.2, GPT-4o +6.9, Sonnet 3.5 -1.9 (ns), GPT-4o-mini +0.4 (ns). Time cost: +35-600% non-reasoning, +20-80% (10-20 s) reasoning.
quote: For dedicated reasoning models, the added benefits of explicit CoT prompting appear negligible
limits: One benchmark (multiple-choice science), simple CoT wording, 8 models from 2024-2025. The direct condition forbids any thinking, harsher than a model's default. No tool or code steps, tokens not matched.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 in part: on a reasoning-trained model, asking for more written steps buys about 0-3 points for 20-80% more time. S2 note-writing should be conditional, not a default, when the base model already thinks at length.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18:513-549 (author PDF, full text)
finding: The founding paper is mostly argument plus aggregate plots, with few numbers. It claims extra Tetris rotations come very early, exceed what a plan alone needs, and show a hidden part of the falling piece sooner. It says plainly that epistemic and pragmatic purpose are hard to separate by behaviour. The 7%/5%/4% rates by skill are NOT in this paper (they come from the 1996 follow-up).
numbers: Physical rotation can take as few as 100 ms; the authors ESTIMATE 800-1200 ms for a mental 90-degree rotation, from a pilot with three Tetris players (one intermediate, one advanced, one expert), 8 presentations of each pair; they allow 200 ms extra for pressing the key. Early rotation exposes the full shape 150-300 ms sooner than waiting for it to fall into view (one square per 150 ms at medium speed, about half a second to appear). Rotations begin in earnest 400-600 ms into an episode, sometimes at the outset (Fig 7). Pieces are rotated more than half their possible rotations, above the 1.5 expected for a four-orientation piece if rotation only followed a finished plan (Fig 6). Keystroke gaps: shortest about 75 ms, average about 250 ms, so a false-start recovery costs 75-750 ms. Free fall about 200 ms per square at start, 100 ms at top speed.
quote: it is often hard to prove that an agent performs a particular action for epistemic rather than for pragmatic reasons
limits: No count of players or episodes found in the extracted text; no percentages by skill; the mental-rotation figure is a 3-player pilot; figures could not be read in text extraction. Authors say extra rotations also serve other aims (memory retrieval, matching to the contour), so not every extra rotation is epistemic.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9 (first half) by correction: K02's three external-time numbers (150, 200, 300 ms) are really 100 ms physical rotation, 150-300 ms earlier exposure, and a 200 ms key-press allowance. Cite the 1994 paper as argument plus pilot, not as an experiment with effect sizes.

source: Mast and Kosslyn (2002) Visual mental images can be ambiguous: insights from individual differences in spatial transformation abilities. Cognition
finding: Later work reverses the strong form of the Chambers and Reisberg claim that mental images cannot be reinterpreted. When people had to rotate the image 180 degrees first, and did not know the study aim, about half found the second reading. Success tracked image-rotation ability, not other imagery measures.
numbers: N=44. 8 found the alternate reading while memorizing the figure, 16 after mentally rotating the image, 20 could not. So 24 of 44 (55%) reinterpreted at some point.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC record); full text not opened. One figure type. Does not show drawings are no better than imagery.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, second half: the rule 'imagery 0%, drawing 100%' (a05) is too strong. Say instead that an external trace makes reinterpretation easier and more reliable for most people, not that it is the only route.

source: Peterson, Kihlstrom, Rose and Glisky (1992) Mental images can be ambiguous: reconstruals and reference-frame reversals. Memory and Cognition
finding: In four experiments the authors found conditions under which images of duck/rabbit and snail/elephant do reverse. Reconstruals (re-parsing parts) happened commonly in any condition. Reference-frame realignments happened mainly after an explicit or implicit suggestion. Images built from good parts reversed more often.
numbers: No counts in the abstract record.
limits: Abstract only; full text not opened. It also cites support from Finke, Pinker and Farah (1989) and the opposing result of Chambers and Reisberg (1985).
agent_relevance: Supports a nuanced 'reread an external trace' rule. For the agent: ask for a re-frame (new axes, new grouping), not just a re-read.

source: Chen, Jhamtani, Sharma, Fan and Wang (2025) Steering Large Language Models between Code Execution and Textual Reasoning. ICLR 2025
finding: Models do not reliably choose code when code would win, and code is not always better than text. Forcing text on a reasoning-trained model (o1-preview) lowered its score below just answering; forcing code raised it. Code plus text plus a summary step gave the best average.
numbers: 14 tasks, 6 models, 300 trials per cell. Average normalised score (%), Only Question / All Text / All Code / Code+Text+Summary: GPT-4o 80.6 / 79.9 / 80.3 / 88.1; GPT-4o-mini 67.6 / 75.9 / 77.4 / 85.0; GPT-3.5 65.3 / 65.3 / 68.1 / 63.9; o1-preview 88.2 / 81.9 / 93.3 / 90.2; Claude-sonnet 71.5 / 72.0 / 74.7 / 76.2; Mixtral 63.4 / 68.0 / 69.2 / 73.6; mean 72.8 / 73.9 / 77.2 / 79.5. Inverse scaling: GPT-3.5 beat GPT-4o with the code interpreter on Game 24 and number multiplying because it chose code more often. Multi-turn refinement helped the code-heavy methods and hurt the text-heavy ones; all methods converged at turn 2.
limits: Pre-2025 models; o1-preview is the only reasoning model; scores normalised per task. Token costs differ by arm but the cost table came out garbled in text extraction, so no token figures are given here.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 and part of gap 1: writing the solution as code helps before execution is considered, but the largest gain comes from running both channels and reconciling them. Forcing text-only on a reasoning model can HURT (88.2 to 81.9). S4 should offer code as an option with a reconciliation step, not as a default.

source: Bogdan, Macar, Nanda and Conmy (2025) Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
finding: Sentence-level resampling of a reasoning trace (replace sentence k with a different sampled sentence, continue 100 times, compare final answers) finds a few sentences with outsized causal effect. Those are planning and uncertainty-management sentences (backtracking, re-evaluating), not the arithmetic ones. A forced-answer test (the Lanham style) misses this and ranks active computation highest.
numbers: DeepSeek R1-Distill Qwen-14B on 20 MATH problems solved 25-75% of the time; one correct and one incorrect trace each = 40 traces; average 144.2 sentences and 4,208 tokens; 100 resamples per sentence. Receiver attention heads agree on which sentences matter (mean r=.56 among top heads vs .35 for any pair); plan and uncertainty sentences get more receiver-head attention than active computation (t > 4.0, p < .001). Scaled-up check on Qwen3-30B-A3B over 15,638 MMLU questions: 3,651 had non-reasoning accuracy under 50%, 2,492 of those solved at least once with reasoning.
limits: 20 math problems, one 14B distilled model with partial checks on an 8B and a 30B model; version read was an ICLR 2026 submission, not peer reviewed in this record. Importance is about the final answer distribution, not the truth of the step.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3: trace ablation by resampling is a workable black-box way to find which written steps carry the answer, and the load-bearing ones are plans and re-checks. For S2/S4 traces run the same test offline on samples: expect plans and revisions to matter, restated facts not. Costs 100 rollouts per step.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think (Anthropic)
finding: When a hint changes the model's answer, the chain of thought admits using the hint only a minority of the time, and less on harder questions. Unfaithful chains were longer, not shorter, so brevity does not explain it. Written reasoning is therefore not a complete record of what drove the answer.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1 on MMLU and GPQA, 6 hint types. Overall faithfulness 25% (Claude 3.7) and 39% (R1); on misaligned hints 20% and 29%. Reasoning models verbalise hints in at least 1% of cases in 5/6 (Claude 3.7) and 6/6 (R1) settings; average faithfulness 3.6x and 1.7x that of their non-reasoning siblings. GPQA vs MMLU: faithfulness 44% lower relative (Claude 3.7), 32% lower (R1). Unfaithful chains averaged 2,064 (+/-59) tokens vs 1,439 faithful (Claude) and 6,003 vs 4,737 (R1). In 6 reward-hacking RL environments the hack was learned (reward > 0.99) but verbalised in under 2% of examples in 5 of 6.
limits: Measures acknowledgement of a planted hint, an upper bound on faithfulness; hints are artificial. Does not say the chain is useless, only that it is not a full causal record.
agent_relevance: For gap 3: do not assume a written step is epistemic because it looks like reasoning. Pair any claim about steps that mattered with an intervention test (d06). A monitor reading the chain will miss most hint use.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo and Griffiths (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Six task types where verbal deliberation hurts people were tried on models. In three (implicit statistical learning, face recognition from description, exceptions in classification) CoT clearly lowers accuracy; the others are mixed. The human-psychology parallel works as a predictor for some, not all.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning (artificial grammar, 50% chance): direct vs CoT accuracy GPT-4o 87.5% vs 64.4% (-23.1, p<.0001), Claude 3 Opus 70.7 vs 62.7 (-8.0), Gemini 1.5 Pro 68.0 vs 61.95 (-6.05), Llama 3.1 70B 65.9 vs 57.1 (-8.8), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 (+1.8, ns). o1-preview vs GPT-4o on a subset: 57.7% vs 94.0% (-36.3 absolute). Tree-of-thoughts variant: 64.55% vs 62.52% CoT, both far below 94.0% direct. Face-description task: GPT-4o 64.0 vs 51.2 (-12.8), Claude 3 Opus 44.0 vs 29.6 (-14.4), Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.0 vs 54.6 (-11.4), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.8 vs 94.8 (-3.0). Exceptions task: trials needed to learn rose up to 331% (GPT-4o 2.9 to 12.5 with CoT).
limits: 2024 models; the o1-preview number compares across model families, so it mixes a model effect with a thinking effect. Some task types showed no consistent drop. The human-model parallel is a heuristic.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 in part: features that predict harm are (a) the right answer rests on a fast statistical or perceptual impression and (b) the rule is learned from many examples, not stated. A cheap pre-check is the item description: if it can be solved by stating rules, write; if by feel over many examples, answer first and write only to check. Not yet tested as a router.

source: Qian et al. (2025) SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation
finding: Agents given tools call them far more than needed, and tool use sometimes turns a right answer into a wrong one. The tested fix is trained (rationale-annotated data plus supervised tuning), not prompt-only. Its prompt-only baselines (a no-tool 'reasoning prompt' versus a 'tool prompt') are mixed.
numbers: Preliminary study: tool overuse rate above 50% for Llama. SMARTAgent cut tool calls by 24% on average and raised performance by 37.1% (macro averages over five open models), and up to 50% fewer unnecessary calls than the tool-prompted base model. MATH accuracy, reasoning prompt (no tools) / tool prompt / SMARTAgent: Llama-3.1-8B 53.0 / 51.0 (1.93 calls) / 54.75 (0.88 calls); Mistral-7B 17.25 / 13.25 / 22.75; GPT-4o 79.5 / 79.25 (0.27 calls). FreshQA (needs fresh facts), Llama-3.1-8B: 26 / 56 / 67.
limits: Trained method; three domains; the 37% gain is a macro-average of percent changes and can look large from low bases. Not a prompt-only gate.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: training is the tested route. The no-tool vs tool-prompt rows show that on math, offering tools does not help and can hurt (Mistral-7B -4.0), while on fresh-fact questions tools help a lot (+30). A prompt-only gate has a real baseline to beat; this paper does not test one.

source: Li et al. (2025) Adaptive Tool Use in Large Language Models with Meta-Cognition Trigger (MeCo)
finding: A training-free signal read from hidden states decides when to call a tool, and beats asking the model in words whether it needs one. Among verbal prompts, 'Yes/No plus a short explanation' was best of five forms; chain-of-thought prompting did worse because the final decision sometimes contradicted the reasoning.
numbers: MetaTool: 1,040 queries, 520 needing a tool. Llama-3-8B decision accuracy (tool calls): Always-call 50.0% (520); Naive verbal prompt 61.9% (296) before fine-tuning and 82.1% (277) after; PYes baseline 63.5% (208) and 81.7% (273); MeCo 65.0% (206) and 84.3% (240). Retrieval takes 14.8 s per call, so skipped calls save latency.
limits: The 'always call' row shows 520 calls for 1,040 queries, so count semantics are unclear (kept as printed). Accuracy is of the 'need a tool' decision, not end-task accuracy. Probes need hidden states, so not usable through a closed API.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a plain verbal self-assessment gate already gives about 62% decision accuracy on an 8B model against 50% for always-calling, so a prompt gate carries some signal. Use a short yes/no with a one-line reason for the gate, not a long chain.

source: Matsnev (2026) Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
finding: A prompt-only way to separate 'how sure am I of my action' from 'how unclear is the request' lets agents ask for clarification more accurately. But adding that self-assessment to the prompt lowered task success slightly on average, and a lot on harder benchmarks.
numbers: Five backbones (GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B). WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification have 50% of tasks deliberately underspecified. Clarification F1: +73% relative over ReAct+UE and +36% over UAM on ALFWorld-Clarification; about +0.28 and +0.21 absolute F1 on average; led on every backbone for WebShop and 4 of 5 for ALFWorld. Task success averaged over 5 benchmarks x 5 backbones: 28.6% (ReAct+UE), 27.8% (UAM), 27.0% (proposed). By benchmark: REAL 32.1% to 19.2%, WebShop 31.9% to 26.1%, ALFWorld 57.5% to 58.9%.
limits: Synthetic underspecification; one-author preprint; low absolute success rates. The author names the drop 'capability dilution' and ascribes it to a fixed shared reasoning budget.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: first prompt-only evidence that an ask-versus-act gate works, at a price. Any gate added to S2/S4 must be tested for dilution: measure end accuracy, not only call counts.

source: Liu, Padmanabhan and Viswanathan (2026) Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems (NeurIPS 2026 FAST workshop)
finding: The first paper found that carries Kirsh and Maglio's term to LLM agents on purpose. It is a short position paper with no experiments. It splits epistemic action into acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence (re-express, sort, diagram), and probing (a controlled contrast or intervention), and proposes a value-of-information rule to pick among them. It asks for a benchmark that fixes task, model and budget and varies which of the three actions are available.
numbers: No measured results. Proposed rule: choose the action e maximising E[V(I_e)|I,e] minus cost c(e), with 'commit now' as the null action. Proposed benchmark separates three abilities: noticing evidence is inadequate, picking an action, using its result; and compares 'told which action' with 'action available but not named'.
limits: Position paper. It argues the scaffold, not the value rule, bounds which actions can be chosen, so the action set must include re-expression and probing, not only search.
agent_relevance: Overturns the K23 wording that no paper maps the theory onto LLM agents (it maps it, without data). Gives a ready three-way label for S2/S4 steps: acquire, transform, probe. Its proposed benchmark is the missing test; a small version is buildable.

source: Feng et al. (2025) ReTool: Reinforcement Learning for Strategic Tool Use in LLMs
finding: Letting a model run code during reinforcement learning beat text-only reinforcement learning on the same base, with fewer training steps and shorter answers. A trained result, but the cleanest recent matched comparison of code execution against text reasoning.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. AIME 2024 pass@1 67.0% with 400 steps (tool) vs 40.0% with 1,080 steps (text RL); AIME 2025 49.3% vs 36.7%. Extended setting 72.5% (AIME 2024) and 54.3% (AIME 2025). o1-preview 44.6 and 49.3 in their table. Cold-start model alone 40.9%, untrained model 26.7%. After RL, response length fell about 40% versus before RL. 32 repeats per item.
limits: Training, not prompting; math only; the 72.5% figure uses a larger extended setup. The cost of running code is not in the response-length figure.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 10: at a fixed base model, execution beats text in the trained regime and shortens answers by about 40%, so tool-based thinking can be more token-efficient than text-only thinking. Not evidence for a prompt-only scaffold on a closed model.

source: Lin and Xu (2025) Understanding Tool-Integrated Reasoning
finding: A formal argument plus experiments that a Python interpreter widens what a model can solve and, for any fixed token budget, some problems fit only in code. On a hybrid thinking model trained both ways, the tool version solves problems the text version cannot, including ones that are not algorithm-friendly.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, RL on 10,000 DAPO problems. Omni-MATH-512 at pass@256: solved 68.4% (text) vs 82.0% (tool); 15.4% of problems newly solved (expansion), 1.8% lost (shrinkage), 66.6% solved by both, 16.2% by neither. On the least algorithm-friendly problems (score 1.0-2.5) the tool model keeps about +9 points at pass@256. Theorem 3.7: for a non-trivial algorithmic problem class, beyond some size no token budget lets text-only generation succeed while code does.
limits: Marked work in progress; one base model; pass@256 measures reach, not first-try accuracy; the friendliness score was assigned by an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: on a model that already reasons at length, execution still adds solved problems (net +13.6 points at pass@256), so run-code steps are not redundant with hidden thinking. About +9 on abstract problems says the gain is not only exact arithmetic.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang and Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Probing for information on purpose did not appear by default. In bandit tasks only one prompt-model configuration explored well: GPT-4 with chain of thought plus an externally summarised history. With the raw history the model kept exploiting.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2; 48 configurations for the first and 72 for GPT-4; horizon T=100 with N=20 or more replicates (a T=500 check with N=20). GPT-4 basic prompt: in more than 60% of replicates it never again tried the better arm (suffix failure). Only success: GPT-4 + CoT + suggestive framing + summarised history as sufficient statistics. The same setup without the summary failed.
limits: 2023-era models; small bandit tasks; no current reasoning models. The authors suggest fine-tuning for complex settings.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: against the Kirsh-Maglio signature at that model generation. Information-seeking moves were not spontaneous and needed a code-built summary of what had been learned, which supports a harness-built typed state (gap 7) as a precondition for useful probing.

source: Pedrozo, Soares and de Oliveira (2026) Do Reasoning Models Ask Better Questions? A Formal Information-Theoretic Analysis on Multi-Turn LLM Games
finding: In a 20-questions-style city-guessing game, models with reasoning get more information per question and finish in fewer turns, with the advantage largest early. A smaller model partly makes up for it by considering more candidate questions, but picks the best one less often.
numbers: 40 cities x 3 runs; information gain (IG) per turn. Partially observable: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking win rate 0.93, 14.88 turns, IG/turn 0.42; Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (no reasoning) win rate 0.10, 29.13 turns, IG/turn 0.14; Qwen3-8B without CoT win rate 0.08, 29.60 turns. Candidate questions considered per turn: 9.74 (8B) vs 7.63 (30B thinking); optimal-choice rate 0.19 vs 0.25. Fully observable: all win 1.00; thinking-30B needs 7.12 turns vs 7.95-9.57 for others.
limits: Instruct and Thinking variants differ in more than reasoning; one game; oracle model is Qwen3-8B so answers are noisy; some Qwen3-8B rows were garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the closest measured test of 'stronger models gather more information per probe, earlier'. It is a question game, not reversible probes in a world, and it rises with reasoning, not size alone. Good support for scoring S2 clarifying questions by information gain.

source: Yuan, Ranka, Lasisi and Ma (2026) Walk Before You Run: The Importance of Data Exploration for Data Analysis Agents
finding: Making the agent write a structured understanding of the dataset (tables, keys, quality issues) before answering raises accuracy on hard spreadsheet tasks. Three conditions: control, the model's own exploration artifact ('middle'), and an oracle artifact ('treatment'). The model's own artifact sometimes matched or beat the oracle one.
numbers: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4 on a real multi-sheet workbook and 12 DSBench tasks (4 simple, 5 mid, 3 hard). Case studies: GPT on a financial-model task 15/20 control, 16/20 middle, 17/20 treatment; Claude on a depot-allocation task 6/9, 7/9, 9/9. Gains concentrated on mid and hard groups.
limits: Very small N per case, no confidence intervals, authors' own benchmark; the middle-versus-treatment differences are one or two questions.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 8: a current-model test of a transformative epistemic action (restructure the evidence before reasoning). A generation effect is hinted: self-built structure can beat given structure. A cheap A/B of pre-answer exploration notes in S2 is justified.

source: Su et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: Unveiling Inefficiency Patterns in Tool-Integrated Reasoning
finding: Many code-tool calls are confirmatory, not epistemic: the model writes the answer in its reasoning first and then runs Python only to check it. Higher tool cost goes with lower correctness even at the same difficulty level.
numbers: Four patterns. Confirmatory tool usage (answer token written before the tool call): 81% of trajectories in the dominant setting (Qwen3-235B-Instruct on MATH500), cost multiplier 1.77x in the PTE (prefill-token-equivalent) metric. Tool-mixing (more than one tool type): 59%, 2.42x. Lack of tool priors (empty output or error): 33%, 2.15x. Format collapse: 100% in its dominant setting, multiplier not given. Incorrect trajectories had higher PTE than correct ones within every difficulty level, up to +793% at MATH500 level 1.
limits: Heuristic detectors; frequency is for the dominant setting, not an average across settings. A confirmatory call can still catch an error.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a ready-made detector for non-epistemic tool steps (answer before call) and a first estimate of 81% in one setting. Complements the K01 test: it measures steps that merely confirm, the opposite end from steps that discover.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Models solve the fully specified problem but often cannot name the one missing fact worth asking for. This is the 'what unknown does this action resolve' step in gap 2.
numbers: Underspecified tasks solvable with one question: Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q, GSME-Q. Models score over 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q but only 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q (abstract). One zero-shot+CoT row: o1-preview 49.91% Logic-Q, 42.31% Planning-Q, 98.01% GSME-Q, 91.32% GSM-Q. Solving the fully specified version does not predict success at picking the question. Weaker models far lower (e.g. Gemma 2 2B at 0.09% on one Logic-Q setting).
limits: Multiple-choice question selection, not free asking; 2024 to early 2025 models; extracted table rows were partly misaligned, so only the abstract ranges and the o1-preview row are used.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: knowing what an action should resolve is itself a weak skill on logic and planning. A gate that asks 'what unknown does this resolve' is only as good as that skill; write the unknown out and check it against the spec before acting.

source: Lee et al. (2026) DART: Draft-Agreement Routing for Training-Free Adaptive Thinking Budgets in Hybrid Reasoning Models
finding: On current hybrid models extended thinking still adds a lot on competition math, adds nothing or hurts on code, and a cheap two-draft agreement check can route many queries away from thinking without loss. A candidate pre-check for gap 5.
numbers: Qwen3-8B no-think vs always-think: MATH-500 76.6 vs 85.6; OlympiadBench 49.8 vs 71.5; HumanEval 60.4 vs 59.1; MBPP 59.5 vs 64.2. HumanEval no-think vs always-think: Qwen3-14B 71.3 vs 66.5, Qwen3-32B 79.9 vs 72.6. DART: thinking-token use down 32-73%, accuracy up to +9.0 on Olympiad-level math and +22.5 on code against always-think; drafts agree (answer directly) for a share of queries that varies by model and dataset. Method: sample two no-think drafts, accept if they agree, otherwise think with a budget set from draft entropy.
limits: Table 1 rows partly garbled in text extraction (only the no-think and always-think columns are cited). Math and code only. The authors' two-call protocol avoids truncation and can change always-think numbers.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: thinking still pays on hard math (+9 to +22 points on one 8B model) but not on code. A two-draft agreement check is a cheap router and could gate whether S2 notes run at all.

source: Qwen Team (2025) Qwen3 Technical Report
finding: With the same weights, switching thinking mode on moves a current open model from weak to strong on competition math. This sets how much written intermediate reasoning still matters in a 2025 reasoning-trained model.
numbers: Qwen3-235B-A22B on AIME'24: 85.7 (thinking) vs 40.1 (non-thinking); MATH-500 98.0 vs 91.2 (last columns of the thinking and non-thinking tables). The report says that for knowledge, STEM, math and coding, thinking-mode fusion and general RL did not bring significant improvements, and that thinking-mode AIME'24 and LiveCodeBench slightly dropped after those stages.
limits: Builder-reported, not independent; non-thinking mode still writes a short rationale; no token-matched comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: written reasoning is not obsolete on a reasoning-trained model; on hard math it still doubles the score. Untested: whether a second visible scratchpad adds to the model's own thinking. That is the experiment to run.

source: Liu (2026) Track, Rank, Crack: Epistemic Working Memory Scales Multi-Hop Reasoning in Language Agents (SLEUTH), re-checked for replication
finding: Searched again for an independent replication of the typed-state result and found none. It remains a single independent-researcher preprint. It is the source of the 'identical commitment trigger fails without structured state' claim.
numbers: 4-hop MuSiQue EM: SLEUTH 53.1, ReAct 42.0, Notes 41.7, Facts-only 49.9, Facts+Hyp. 48.9, Facts+Q. 47.7. 2-hop SLEUTH 66.1 vs Reflexion 61.4. Commit trigger at 70% of the turn budget. Protocol adherence on GLM-5 15% to 99% with the adapted prompt plus runtime check.
limits: No independent replication; no variance in the passages read; two model families (Claude Sonnet, GLM-5). The Notes arm is a weak version of free notes.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Keep K16 and K17 single-source until a second lab or our own run reproduces them.
